entities.summary:
The St. Paulus Dom (Cathedral of Saint Paul) in Münster, Germany, is a Westphalian Romanesque-Gothic cathedral built between 1225 and 1265 CE and one of the most historically significant buildings in Germany due to its role as the site of the Peace of Westphalia negotiations (1648) — the treaties that ended the Thirty Years' War and created the modern state system. The cathedral's St. Paul's Chamber (Friedenssaal, or Hall of Peace) is where delegations from Spain, France, the Holy Roman Empire, Sweden, and the German states negotiated the peace that shaped European political order for centuries.

The cathedral was originally built in the Romanesque style but transitional Gothic elements were incorporated during construction. Its most famous feature is the astronomic clock (1540 CE) — one of the most complex medieval astronomical clocks in the world, combining calendar, astronomical, and mechanical functions with automated figures processing daily at noon. The clock survived the massive Allied bombing of Münster in 1944 that destroyed 90% of the city.

The Peace of Westphalia (1648) negotiations in Münster (and simultaneously in Osnabrück) are considered the foundation of the Westphalian system — the principle of national sovereignty and non-interference in internal affairs that became the basis of international law. The treaties recognized Protestant states in the Holy Roman Empire, established religious tolerance principles, and created the balance-of-power framework in Europe. The Friedenssaal (Hall of Peace) preserves the portraits of all 246 peace delegates.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: St. Paulus Dom in Münster hosted the Peace of Westphalia negotiations that created the Westphalian system of national sovereignty — the foundation of international law still governing relations between states 375 years later.
